title: Comparison of Weekly Training Load and Acute: Chronic Workload Ratio Methods to Estimate Change in Training Load in Running
authors: Cloosterman KLA, de Vos RJ, van Oeveren B, Visser E, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, van Middelkoop M
population: Dutch recreational runners registered for 10-42.195 km events who shared GPS data (73.3% men, mean age 44.3 y); descriptive epidemiology within an RCT dataset, no injury outcome
findings: 430 runners, 22,839 training sessions, distance-based; a significant load increase was predefined as weekly load progression of 30% or more, or ACWR of 1.5 or more.

Share of sessions classified as significant increases: weekly load method 33.4% (95% CI 32.8-34.0), coupled rolling average 16.2% (15.7-16.6), uncoupled rolling average 25.8% (25.3-26.4), EWMA 18.9% (18.4-19.4).
43.0% of the flagged sessions from the weekly method were different from the coupled rolling average and EWMA methods.
Sessions flagged by the coupled rolling average showed 100% overlap with the uncoupled rolling average and EWMA flags.

Authors conclude the difference between the weekly method and the ACWR methods is high and that research on the association between these measures and injury is needed to validate a measure of load change in runners.
limitations: Describes how often each method flags a session; no injury outcome, so it says nothing about which flag is right. Distance-only, event-registered Dutch runners.
implications: The reference window and calculation method decide which sessions are flagged: the same 30% / 1.5 cutoffs flag 16%-33% of sessions depending on method. Document the exact window (calendar week, trailing 30 days) for every ramp and spike rule and test it on the same logs.

A weekly 30% flag fires about 1.8-2 times as often as the coupled rolling-average or EWMA ACWR 1.5 flag in this dataset; consider suppressing the hard ramp after a recent low-volume week (a design choice, not a finding).
